pre.one: The opening words set out the aim: to stop the same income being taxed twice by Saudi Arabia and {P}. Newer treaties add a second aim: not to create chances to pay little or no tax through evasion or avoidance.
pts: The preamble has no rules of its own, but tax authorities and courts read the articles in the light of the aim it states.
Where the preamble mentions treaty shopping, using the treaty to pass benefits to people in a third country is against its purpose.

1.one: Only people and companies that are resident in Saudi Arabia, in {P}, or in both. What counts is residence, not nationality.
pts: Article 4 (Resident) says who counts as a resident.
Someone resident in neither country cannot use the treaty, even if the money passes through one of them.
1.ex: A company resident in {P} that earns fees from a Saudi customer can rely on this treaty. A company resident in a third country cannot, even if it is paid into a bank account in {P}.
1.tip: To claim the treaty in Saudi Arabia you need a tax residency certificate issued by the other country's tax authority.

2.q: Which taxes does the treaty deal with?
2.one: The income taxes of both countries, and taxes on capital where a country has them. On the Saudi side every treaty in this library names zakat and income tax; withholding tax is collected as part of income tax.
pts: VAT, customs duties and excise tax are not covered.
A similar tax that either country brings in later is covered automatically, and each tax authority tells the other about important changes.
2.tip: A tax being covered does not mean it is waived. It means the treaty's rules decide how much of it each country may charge.

3.q: What do the main words mean?
3.one: This article explains words the treaty uses throughout, such as person, company, enterprise, international traffic, national and competent authority.
pts: It sets the geographical meaning of Saudi Arabia and of {P}, including sea areas where each has sovereign rights.
It names the competent authority, the official in each country who runs the treaty. For Saudi Arabia this is the Minister of Finance or an authorised representative.
A word the treaty does not define takes its meaning from the tax law of the country applying the treaty.

4.q: Which country counts as your home under the treaty?
4.one: You are resident in a country if its law taxes you because you live there or, for a company, because it was set up or is managed there. If both countries treat you as resident, a tie-breaker picks one.
pts: For a person, the tie-breaker asks in turn: where is your permanent home, where are your personal and economic ties closer, where do you usually live, and which country's national are you? If that still does not decide it, the two tax authorities agree between them.
For a company, most treaties pick the place of effective management: where the key management and business decisions are really made.
Most Saudi treaties also count the government itself and its local authorities as residents, and some add state-owned or tax-exempt funds.
4.tip: Residence decides which treaty applies and which country has the first right to tax most income, so it is the first thing to settle.

5.q: When does a business from one country have a taxable presence in the other?
5.one: A business from {P} pays Saudi tax on its business profits only if it has a permanent establishment (PE) in Saudi Arabia. The same rule protects Saudi businesses working in {P}.
pts: A fixed place of business, such as an office, branch, factory, workshop or mine, is a PE.
A building, construction or installation project becomes a PE only if it lasts longer than the time limit in the treaty.
Many Saudi treaties also create a PE when staff provide services in the country for longer than a set number of days or months.
Someone who regularly concludes contracts in the country for the business can create a PE. A genuinely independent agent acting in the ordinary course of business does not.
Places used only for storage, display, buying or other preparatory or supporting work are not a PE.
5.ex: A contractor from {P} installs equipment at a plant in Jubail for four months. Under a six-month limit the site is not a PE, so Saudi Arabia cannot tax the contractor's profit from the job under this treaty.
5.tip: Keep records of days on site and days staff spend in the country. Time on connected projects can be added together.

6.q: Who taxes income from land and buildings?
6.one: The country where the property is may tax the income from it, such as rent or farming income. The owner's home country may tax it too, but must then give relief for the tax paid where the property is.
pts: Immovable property takes the meaning it has in the law of the country where it is. It always includes land, buildings, rights to mineral deposits and other natural resources.
Ships and aircraft are not immovable property.
The rule applies whether the owner uses the property, rents it out or uses it some other way.
6.ex: A resident of {P} who owns a flat in Jeddah and rents it out can be taxed on the rent in Saudi Arabia.

7.q: Where are a business's profits taxed?
7.one: Only in the country where the business is resident, unless it has a PE in the other country. If it has one, that other country may tax the profits that belong to the PE, not the profits of the whole business.
pts: The PE's profits are worked out as if it were a separate business dealing at market prices with the rest of the company.
Costs incurred for the PE, including a fair share of head office costs, can be deducted.
Where the profits include income that has its own article, such as dividends or royalties, that article applies instead.
7.ex: A {P} company has a branch in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia taxes the branch's profits. Profits the company earns at home from customers in other countries stay outside Saudi tax.
7.tip: No PE usually means no Saudi tax on business profits under the treaty. The Saudi payer may still have to withhold tax under Saudi law; the treaty relief is then claimed through ZATCA.

8.q: Who taxes airlines and shipping lines?
8.one: Profits from running ships or aircraft in international traffic are taxed only in one country: usually where the operator's effective management is, or under some treaties where the operator is resident.
pts: This normally covers chartering out ships or aircraft and using containers, where this goes with the transport business.
Some Saudi treaties extend the rule to road transport.
The same rule applies to profits from pools, joint businesses and international operating agencies.
8.ex: Profits that a {P} airline earns from passengers flying out of Saudi Arabia are taxed only in its home country under this article.

9.q: What if related companies trade at prices that are not market prices?
9.one: Each country may adjust the profits of related businesses to what they would have been had the businesses dealt with each other like unrelated parties. This is the treaty basis for transfer pricing.
pts: If one country increases a company's profits this way, paragraph 2 (where the treaty has it) asks the other country to reduce the related company's profits to match, so the same profit is not taxed twice.
9.ex: ZATCA increases a Saudi subsidiary's profit by 8 because it paid its {P} parent 20 for services worth 12. {P} should then reduce the parent's taxable profit by the same 8.
9.tip: If the other country does not make the matching adjustment, ask for it through the mutual agreement procedure.

10.q: How are dividends paid across the border taxed?
10.one: The shareholder's home country may tax the dividend. The country where the paying company is resident may also tax it, but not above the rate in this treaty.
pts: The cap applies only if the person receiving the dividend is its beneficial owner: the person who really owns it, not a nominee or agent.
In Saudi Arabia the paying company withholds the tax from the payment. Saudi law's own rate on dividends paid to non-residents is 5%.
If the shares belong to a PE the shareholder has in the company's country, the dividend is taxed as part of the PE's profits instead.

11.one: Many Saudi treaties call interest 'income from debt-claims'. The lender's home country may tax it. The country where it arises may also tax it up to the treaty rate; some treaties exempt it there completely.
pts: Saudi law's own rate on loan returns paid to non-residents is 5%. The treaty can lower it, sometimes to 0%.
The treaty rate applies only to the beneficial owner.
Penalties for late payment are not treated as interest.
If the interest is higher than an unrelated lender would charge, the treaty rate applies only to the normal amount.

12.one: Royalties are payments for using intellectual property, such as software licences, trademarks, patents and know-how, and in many Saudi treaties for using equipment. The owner's country may tax them, and the country where they arise may also tax them up to the treaty rate.
pts: Saudi law's own rate on royalties paid to non-residents is 15%. The treaty usually lowers it.
Some treaties set a lower rate for renting industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.
A royalty arises in Saudi Arabia when the payer is resident there, or when a PE in Saudi Arabia bears the cost.
Fees for services are not royalties just because they use expertise. They are usually business profits, unless the treaty has a separate article on technical services.

12A.q: How are fees for technical services taxed?
12A.one: This treaty has a separate article for managerial, technical and consultancy fees. The country where the fees arise may tax them up to the treaty rate, even if the provider has no PE there.
pts: It follows the UN Model approach (Article 12A). Under the OECD approach these fees would be business profits, taxed where they arise only through a PE.
Pay to employees, fees for teaching at educational institutions and payments by individuals for personal services are excluded.
Saudi law's own rate on technical and consulting services paid to non-residents is 5%. A treaty never increases tax, so Saudi withholding stays at 5% where the treaty rate is higher.

13.q: Who taxes gains from selling assets?
13.one: It depends on the asset. Saudi treaties differ most on gains from selling shares, so read this article closely.

14.one: Income of independent professionals, such as doctors, lawyers, engineers, architects and accountants, is taxed in their home country. The other country may tax it only if they have a fixed base there or, under many Saudi treaties, stay there beyond a set number of days.
pts: Where one of those tests is met, the other country may tax only the income from the work done there or linked to the fixed base.
The OECD Model dropped this article in 2000 and now treats such income as business profits under Articles 5 and 7. Many Saudi treaties keep it.
14.ex: An architect resident in {P} spends 50 days in Riyadh on a project and has no office there. Under a 183-day rule, only {P} may tax the fee.

15.one: In the employee's home country, unless the work is done in the other country. Even then, the home country keeps the sole right to tax if all three short-stay conditions are met.
pts: The employee is in the other country for no more than the day limit in the treaty, counted over the period the treaty sets.
The employer is not resident in that other country.
The pay is not borne by a PE or fixed base the employer has in that other country.
15.ex: An engineer employed and resident in {P} works on a project in Dammam for 60 days, paid from {P} and not charged to any Saudi PE. All three conditions are met, so only {P} may tax that salary.
15.tip: Pay for work on ships and aircraft in international traffic follows a separate rule in this article.

16.one: Fees paid to a member of a company's board of directors may be taxed in the country where the company is resident, wherever the board meets.
16.ex: A resident of {P} who sits on the board of a Saudi company may be taxed in Saudi Arabia on the board fees.
16.tip: Pay for a separate executive job at the company normally falls under the employment article instead.

17.q: How are performers and athletes taxed on tours?
17.one: Performers and athletes may be taxed where they perform, even on a short visit and without a PE. This also applies where the fee is paid to their company or agent rather than to them.
pts: Many Saudi treaties exempt visits that are funded mainly from public money of the home country or take place under a cultural agreement between the two governments.
17.ex: A band from {P} paid for a concert in Riyadh may be taxed in Saudi Arabia on that fee.

18.one: Pensions for past private employment are usually taxed only in the country where the pensioner lives.
pts: Pensions paid by a government for government service usually follow the government service article.
Some treaties give social security pensions to the country that pays them. Check this article for the rule in this treaty.

19.one: Pay and pensions that a government pays for government work are usually taxed only by that government's country.
pts: The exception is local staff: if the work is done in the other country by someone resident there who is its national, or who did not move there just for the job, only that other country may tax the pay.
Pay for work in a business run by a government is taxed like private pay.
19.ex: A {P} civil servant posted to Riyadh is taxed only by {P} on the government salary.

20.q: Are students taxed on money from home?
20.one: Students and trainees from one country who are in the other only to study or train are not taxed there on payments from abroad for their living costs, studies or training.
pts: Some treaties also exempt limited earnings from work during the stay. Check the conditions in this article.
20.ex: A student from {P} at a Saudi university who receives money from home for living costs is not taxed in Saudi Arabia on it.

teachers.q: Are visiting teachers and researchers taxed?
teachers.one: Many Saudi treaties exempt visiting teachers and researchers in the host country on pay for their teaching or research. This article has no equivalent in the OECD Model.
pts: The conditions differ from treaty to treaty: some set a time limit, some require an invitation from a university or the government, and some apply only to pay from abroad. Read the text.

21.q: What about income that no other article covers?
21.one: Income that no other article deals with is taxed only in the recipient's home country, unless it belongs to a PE in the other country.
pts: Some Saudi treaties also let the country where the income arises tax it. Check this article's text.
21.tip: This is the catch-all article, so check first whether a more specific article applies.

22.one: Where a country taxes capital or wealth, this article splits the right to tax it the same way as income: property where it is, business assets where the PE is, and everything else in the owner's home country.
pts: It matters only where one of the two countries has a tax on capital.

23.q: If both countries tax the same income, how is the double tax removed?
23.one: The home country gives relief for the tax paid in the other country, usually as a credit against its own tax on the same income. The credit cannot be more than the home country's own tax on that income.
pts: Saudi Arabia gives a credit for tax paid in {P} on income that the treaty lets {P} tax.
Some partner countries exempt the income instead of giving a credit; the article says which method each country uses.
Many Saudi treaties state that this article does not change how zakat is collected.
23.ex: A Saudi company earns 100 in {P}, which taxes it at 10. Saudi tax on that income would be 20, so Saudi Arabia allows a credit of 10 and the company pays 10 more. Total tax is 20, not 30.

25.q: What can you do if a country taxes you against the treaty?
25.one: You can ask a competent authority (the tax authority that runs the treaty) to take up your case. If it cannot fix the problem itself, it tries to agree a solution with the other country's authority.
pts: The case must be presented within the time limit in the treaty, counted from the first notice of the tax that breaks the treaty.
You can use this procedure as well as appeals under local law.
An agreement is put into effect even if local time limits have passed.
The authorities must try to agree, but they are not obliged to reach agreement.
In Saudi Arabia, requests go to ZATCA, which publishes guidance on how to apply.

26.q: Can the two tax authorities share information about you?
26.one: Yes. They exchange information that may be relevant to applying the treaty or their own tax laws, and must keep it as secret as their own tax information.
pts: Under most newer treaties, a country cannot refuse just because a bank holds the information.
A country does not have to give information that would reveal trade secrets or go against public policy.
26.tip: Assume that what you tell one tax authority can reach the other.

28.q: Does the treaty change diplomatic tax privileges?
28.one: No. Tax privileges that diplomats and consular staff have under international law or special agreements continue to apply.

29.one: This article usually holds anti-abuse rules. Benefits can be refused where getting them was one of the main purposes of an arrangement, and each country's own anti-avoidance rules still apply.
pts: It may also hold other rules agreed for this treaty only, so read the text.
Through the multilateral instrument (MLI), a main-purpose test can also apply to a treaty whose own text does not contain one, where both countries have listed the treaty.

30.q: Which territories does the treaty cover?
30.one: This article sets out the territories the treaty applies to.

31.q: From when does the treaty apply?
31.one: This article says when the treaty came into force and when it began to apply: usually to withholding taxes on amounts paid from 1 January after entry into force, and to other taxes for tax years starting on or after that date.

32.one: The treaty stays in force until one country ends it with written notice through diplomatic channels. Notice is usually allowed only after a minimum number of years and by a set date in the year; the treaty then stops applying from the following year.

govinv.one: This article exempts investment income that one country's government earns in the other country, including through its central bank and wholly owned public bodies.
pts: The bodies and the income covered differ by treaty. Some exclude income from land and buildings.

special.one: This article holds rules agreed for this treaty only. Read the text to see what it covers.

headings.one: The headings are there to help the reader and do not change the meaning of the articles.

prot.one: The protocol is part of the treaty. It adds to, explains or changes the articles, so always read it with the article it refers to.

claim.t: Claiming a treaty rate in Saudi Arabia
claim.src: ZATCA, Tax Circular on WHT under Double Taxation Agreements, version of 1 January 2025, sections 4.1–4.2
pts: The claim is made through ZATCA's portal, in one of two ways: the payer applies the treaty rate when paying, or withholds at the Saudi rate and the non-resident claims a refund.
Both ways need a tax residency certificate from the other country's tax authority in its own format, the request on ZATCA's form, and attestation by the embassy or an apostille.

Applying the rate when paying also needs an undertaking on Form Q/7C. A refund also needs the payer's authorisation, the withholding return and payment receipt, and a letter attested by the Chamber of Commerce.
The time limit to apply, and for ZATCA to review the claim, is five years.

gen.note: Plain-language summary to help you read the treaty. It is not the treaty text and not tax advice. The treaty text governs.

inherit.q: Does this treaty cover inheritance tax?
inherit.one: Yes. Unusually, this treaty also covers inheritance tax. This article decides which country may tax property passed on at death; for example, land and buildings are taxed only where they are.

refunds.q: What if too much tax was withheld?
refunds.one: Tax withheld at source above what the treaty allows is refunded on request, made by the taxpayer or by the taxpayer's home country. The article sets the conditions and time limits.

sparing.q: What happens to tax reliefs given under investment laws?
sparing.one: Tax that one country waived or reduced for a limited period under its investment incentive laws is treated as if it had been paid, so the other country still gives credit for it. Without this rule, the home country would collect the tax the incentive was meant to save.
